title: Matrices
summary: Matrices add only when they have the same shape, multiply only when the inner dimensions agree, and reverse order under transpose and inverse. Multiplication is not commutative.
intuition:
A matrix is a rectangular array, and every legal operation first checks the shape. Two matrices add, and a matrix is transposed, entry by entry. The transpose turns an $m\times n$ matrix into an $n\times m$ matrix by swapping $(i,j)$ with $(j,i)$. Multiplication is the operation with a real constraint: $A$ must be $m\times n$ and $B$ must be $n\times p$, and the product $AB$ is then $m\times p$. The inner dimensions have to be the same number. When they are, the $(i,j)$ entry of $AB$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$.

Order matters. Even when $AB$ and $BA$ both exist they need not be equal, and when $A$ is $2\times 3$ and $B$ is $3\times 2$ the two products have different shapes, $2\times 2$ against $3\times 3$, so they cannot be equal. The transpose reverses a product, $(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$, for the same reason the inverse does: $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$ when $A$ and $B$ are invertible matrices of the same size. Putting the factors back in the original order is the standard mistake.

A square matrix has a two-sided inverse exactly when it has full rank, that is, rank $n$ for an $n\times n$ matrix. A non-square matrix never has a two-sided inverse. Full column rank gives a left inverse built from $A^\top A$, and full row rank gives a right inverse; those one-sided inverses are not the object this lesson calls $A^{-1}$.

definitions.body: Matrices $A$ and $B$ may be added only when they have the same number of rows and the same number of columns. The transpose $A^\top$ satisfies $(A^\top)_{ij}=A_{ji}$, and $(A+B)^\top=A^\top+B^\top$.

If $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times p$, the product $AB$ is the $m\times p$ matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is row $i$ of $A$ dotted with column $j$ of $B$. If the inner dimensions differ, $AB$ is undefined.
A square matrix $A$ is invertible when there exists $A^{-1}$ with $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I$. For an $n\times n$ real matrix this happens exactly when $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$.

formulas.name: Transpose of a product
formulas.note: The order reverses. The same pattern holds for a longer product: $(ABC)^\top=C^\top B^\top A^\top$.

formulas.name: Inverse of a product
formulas.note: Both factors are square and invertible. The order reverses. It is not $A^{-1}B^{-1}$.

formulas.name: Shape of a product
formulas.note: The inner dimensions must agree. Addition needs both matrices to be $m\times n$.

properties: Matrix multiplication is associative and distributes over addition. It is not commutative: $AB$ and $BA$ may both exist and still differ, or only one of them may exist.
$(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$, and $(A+B)^\top=A^\top+B^\top$ when the sum exists.
When $A$ and $B$ are invertible and the same size, $AB$ is invertible and $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$.
A square matrix has a two-sided inverse if and only if it has full rank. A non-square matrix does not have a two-sided inverse.
$AB=0$ does not force $A=0$ or $B=0$. A nonzero matrix can kill a nonzero vector, and the same idea builds a product of nonzero matrices.

examples.title: Two products, the reversed transpose, and the reversed inverse
steps: The product $AB$ has entries $1\cdot 1+2\cdot 3=7$, $1\cdot 0+2\cdot 1=2$, $0\cdot 1+1\cdot 3=3$, and $0\cdot 0+1\cdot 1=1$, so $AB=\begin{pmatrix}7&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$.
The other order is $BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&7\end{pmatrix}$. The $(2,2)$ entry alone, $3\cdot 2+1\cdot 1=7$, already shows $BA\neq AB$.

$(AB)^\top=\begin{pmatrix}7&3\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$. And $B^\top A^\top=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7&3\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, the same matrix. Since $\det(AB)=7-6=1$, the inverse is $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-3&7\end{pmatrix}$, which equals $B^{-1}A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-3&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

examples.title: Inner dimensions and two different shapes
examples.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $AB$ and $BA$, and say why neither addition nor equality of the two products is legal.
steps: $A$ is $2\times 3$ and $B$ is $3\times 2$, so both products exist. $AB$ is $2\times 2$ and $BA$ is $3\times 3$.
$BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. A $2\times 2$ matrix and a $3\times 3$ matrix cannot be equal and cannot be added.
examples.answer: $AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Different shapes: not equal, and not addable.

traps: Writing $(AB)^{-1}=A^{-1}B^{-1}$. The inverse reverses the order, just as the transpose does. Check on the matrices above: $A^{-1}B^{-1}$ is not $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-3&7\end{pmatrix}$.
Cancelling a common factor in $AB=AC$. From $A(B-C)=0$ you may not conclude $B=C$ unless $A$ is invertible, or at least has a left inverse.
Adding matrices of different shapes, or multiplying when the columns of the first matrix are not exactly the rows of the second.
Expanding $(A+B)^2$ as $A^2+2AB+B^2$. The cross terms are $AB+BA$, and they agree only when the two matrices commute.
python:
def mul(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

def T(A):
    return [list(row) for row in zip(*A)]

A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]]
B = [[1, 0], [3, 1]]
AB = mul(A, B)
BA = mul(B, A)
assert AB == [[7, 2], [3, 1]]
assert BA == [[1, 2], [3, 7]]
assert AB != BA
assert T(AB) == mul(T(B), T(A))
Ainv = [[1, -2], [0, 1]]
Binv = [[1, 0], [-3, 1]]
assert mul(Binv, Ainv) == [[1, -2], [-3, 7]]
A23 = [[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1]]
B32 = [[1, 2], [0, 1], [1, 0]]
assert mul(A23, B32) == [[2, 2], [1, 1]]
assert mul(B32, A23) == [[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1]]
print(AB[0][0])

questions.stem: $A$ is $2\times 3$ and $B$ is $3\times 4$. The product $AB$ is
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. The inner dimensions are both $3$, so the product exists and its shape is the outer dimensions: $2$ rows from $A$ and $4$ columns from $B$. Option A would be the shape of a product of two $3$-column objects that this pair is not. $BA$ is the product that is undefined, because $4\neq 2$.

questions.stem: If $A$ and $B$ are invertible matrices of the same size, then $(AB)^{-1}$ equals
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. Multiply $AB$ on the left by $B^{-1}A^{-1}$: the inner $BB^{-1}$ cancels first, then $AA^{-1}$, leaving $I$. The reversed order $A^{-1}B^{-1}$ is the inverse of $BA$, not of $AB$. The transpose identity is a different reversal, $(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$, and it is not the inverse.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: $(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$ whenever the product $AB$ is defined.
Matrix multiplication is commutative for all square matrices.
$(A+B)^\top=A^\top+B^\top$ when $A$ and $B$ have the same shape.
An $n\times n$ matrix has a two-sided inverse if and only if its rank is $n$.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, C, and D**. The transpose reverses products and respects sums. Full rank is the condition for a square matrix to be invertible. B is false: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ give $AB=\begin{pmatrix}7&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&7\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, C, and D**. The four entries of $AB$ are $7,2,3,1$. The general identity $(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$ applies, and a direct multiply gives $\begin{pmatrix}7&3\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ on both sides. $A\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I$. But $BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&7\end{pmatrix}$, which is not $AB$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$. Enter the $(1,1)$ entry of $AB$.
questions.solution: The answer is **7**. The $(1,1)$ entry is row $1$ of $A$ dotted with column $1$ of $B$: $(1)(1)+(2)(3)=1+6=7$. The full product is $\begin{pmatrix}7&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$.
